To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a digital rectal examination (DRE) performed by a trained urologist is a good predictor of prostate cancer (PC) in men with a serum PSA between 3.0 and 10.0 ng/ml, and that a DRE is not a good predictor for the presence of a Gleason score of 7 or higher PC.

a positive DRE is a strong predictor for the presence of high grade prostate cancer, and that the presence of high-grade prostate cancer is an independent predictor for the presence and extent of extracapsular extension of the tumor, and for positive lymph nodes.

(a) in a large screening population, a positive DRE is an independent predictor for the presence of clinically significant prostate cancer, and (b) the predictive value of a positive DRE depends on the PSA level.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how prostate cancer screening can be improved.
prostate cancer detection and treatment.

the evaluation of the diagnostic performance of digital rectal examination (DRE), prostate specific antigen (PSA) and transrectal ultrasound guided prostate biopsy (TRUSPB) for the diagnosis of prostate carcinoma in the European Randomised study of Screening for Prostrate Cancer (ERSPC).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results of the ERSPCs are not only very promising, but also very encouraging.
a positive DRE is a significant risk factor for prostate cancer.
a DRE is an important and necessary part of the initial work-up of the patient suspected of harbouring prostate cancer, but it is not a sufficient tool to diagnose or exclude prostate cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ERSPC is an excellent example of the way that a well-designed randomized trial should be performed and analyzed.
digital rectal examination (DRE) has a low sensitivity for the detection of clinically significant cancer.
the digital rectal exam is not an important part of the screening process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the digital rectal examination, when done correctly, can identify a substantial fraction of cancers missed by PSA screening.
the risk of prostate cancer is higher in patients with abnormal digital rectal exam (DRE) than in patients with normal DRE.
